text:
Under almost every big department store in Japan there's a basement with dozens of food counters, free tastings and price stickers that come out in the last hour. Here's how to walk one like a regular 👇

🤔 Guess first: which counters get the discount stickers first? The answer is here 👉 https://japanbystation.com/depachika-japan-food-halls-how-they-work

We took our time with this one and checked the hours, prices and the new tax rules against the stores' own pages and Japan's tourism agency.

🍡 WHAT'S DOWN THERE

1️⃣ Sweets first. Pâtisseries on one side, wagashi and tea on the other. At Nihonbashi Mitsukoshi, Toraya's bamboo-wrapped yokan is ¥3,024, the kind of box people carry home with both hands.

2️⃣ Bento and deli. Isetan Shinjuku has about 50 deli and bento shops. Daimaru Tokyo, right on top of Tokyo Station, says it brings in about 1,000 new bento a year. That's your Shinkansen lunch sorted.

3️⃣ The fresh market. Fruit, fish and wagyu sold like jewellery. Free samples pop up here, from ham to oden.

⏰ THE LAST HOUR

No store publishes a time, but Time Out Tokyo suggests going 30 to 60 minutes before closing, when most ready-to-eat food is marked down. Sweets keep longer, so they rarely drop.

🍽️ AND UPSTAIRS

Take the lift to the top: Isetan's Eat Paradise on 7F runs to 22:00, and Daimaru Tokyo's 13F to 23:00.

Our take: sweets and gifts in the morning when the shelves are full, dinner in the last hour.
